opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think "best possible" is doing a lot of work there. If you mean the ceiling, the behavior you'd get if you could think as long as you wanted about every decision, that's just a very high bar. Almost any interesting decision has a huge space of possible actions and consequences, and you can always get a bit better by thinking more: considering more options, modeling other agents more carefully, checking your reasoning, running more simulations of how things might go. There isn't an obvious point where returns go to zero.

You can see this in domains we understand well. In chess or Go, you keep getting stronger as you throw more search at the problem, and those are tiny, clean environments compared to the real world. In the real world you also have to model other minds, and some of them are modeling you back, which is a big source of computational blowup.

So my view isn't that intelligence is mysterious or needs some special ingredient. It's that the gap between "pretty good" and "as good as possible" is enormous, and closing it is mostly about compute. Humans are somewhere on that curve. I'd guess we're quite far from the top, and I don't think evolution had much reason to push us close to it.

That's one reason I'm skeptical of stories where a system gets a little smarter than humans and then very quickly becomes something like optimal. I think there's a lot of room above us, but getting further up that curve gets increasingly expensive. That matters a lot for how fast and how smoothly things go.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions considering options, modeling consequences, and running simulations, but does not propose simulating every possible universe.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So I think the basic intuition is that almost any decision you could make, you can do better at it by thinking longer about it. Like, if I'm trying to decide what to say right now, I could spend a second, or I could spend an hour considering all the ways the conversation might go, what you're likely to ask next, what the audience is going to take away from it. And the hour version is just going to be better. Not infinitely better, but better. And that's true of basically every decision, at every level of granularity, and the returns don't really stop anywhere obvious.

So if you ask what the best behavior is, in some idealized sense, you're sort of asking what you'd do with an unbounded amount of deliberation. And that's a thing that no physical system can actually implement. Every real agent, including humans, including whatever AI systems we build, is making a tradeoff where it spends some amount of compute on a decision and then just goes. Most of what intelligence looks like in practice is being good at that tradeoff — knowing when to stop, having cheap heuristics that get you most of the way there, caching the results of past thinking so you don't have to redo it.

I think this matters for how I think about AI, because it means there isn't really a ceiling you hit where you've "solved" intelligence. There's always this gradient where more compute buys you more. So the question is never "is this system as smart as it could possibly be," it's "how efficiently does it convert compute into good decisions, and how does that compare to the alternatives." And it's also part of why I'm somewhat skeptical of pictures where you have a very small system that's just arbitrarily competent — like, there's probably a lot of structure in the world, and a lot of it you only get to exploit by actually doing the computation.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes extended deliberation and considering possible conversation outcomes, but does not propose simulating every possible universe.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think there’s a particular level of computation where you’ve suddenly gotten the best possible behavior. You can keep spending more computation to consider more possibilities, to think further ahead, to check whether your reasoning was actually right.

Take chess. The rules are incredibly simple, and we know an algorithm that would play optimally: you can just search the entire game tree. But doing that is totally infeasible. So the interesting question is how close you can get with the computation you actually have. And intelligence in the real world seems much more like that, except you don’t even have a clean specification of the game or know all the possible moves.

That doesn’t mean you need an enormous amount of computation to outperform humans. Humans are operating under very severe constraints, and there could be much better ways to use the same resources. I’d distinguish pretty sharply between being better than a human and doing the best thing that could possibly be done.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses exhaustive search of the chess game tree as infeasible, but does not propose simulating every possible universe.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, even if you understand the world perfectly, you can still spend more computation figuring out what to do. Suppose you’re designing a computer chip. You could consider a design, work out how well it performs, and then consider another design. Having a better understanding of physics helps you evaluate those designs more efficiently, but it doesn’t mean you immediately know which design is best.

And the space of possible designs is enormous. So I don’t think there’s some relatively small amount of computation after which you’ve exhausted all the useful thinking you could do. You can keep searching, keep discovering better strategies, keep working out consequences that you hadn’t worked out before.

That’s different from saying that getting to human-level performance has to be expensive. There may be very efficient ways to do that. But the best possible behavior is a much stronger standard. You’re asking whether any additional thinking could improve your decision, and in a complicated world, I’d expect the answer to remain yes for a very long time.

r001.rationale: The response describes searching a large space of possible chip designs and strategies, but does not propose simulating every possible universe.
